question: Which of the following expresses the sinusoidal AC voltage v(t) = 100√2 sin(ωt + π/6) [V] as a phasor (polar form) whose magnitude is the RMS value?
explanation: Method 1 (from the definition): the magnitude of the phasor is the RMS value, the peak value 100√2 V divided by √2, which is 100 V. The angle is the initial phase π/6 rad = 30°, so the phasor is 100∠30° V. Method 2 (check with complex numbers): 100∠30° = 100(cos 30° + j sin 30°) = 86.6 + j50 V; multiplying by √2 and e^(jωt) and taking the imaginary part gives back the original v(t). In circuit calculations it is usual to use the RMS value, not the peak value, as the magnitude of a phasor.
choiceNotes: π/6 rad is 30°, not 60°. Since π rad = 180°, π/6 rad = 180° ÷ 6 = 30°.
Correct. It is the phasor with an RMS value of 100 V and a phase of 30°.
141 V is the peak value 100√2 V, not the RMS value. Some texts use the peak value as the phasor magnitude, but this question asks for the RMS value.

question: Which of the following is the admittance Y of a load whose impedance is Z = 3 + j4 [Ω]?
explanation: Method 1 (rationalizing the denominator): multiplying the numerator and denominator of Y = 1/(3 + j4) by the complex conjugate 3 − j4 gives Y = (3 − j4)/(3² + 4²) = (3 − j4)/25 = 0.12 − j0.16 S. Method 2 (polar form): |Z| = √(3² + 4²) = 5 Ω and the angle is about 53.1°, so Y = (1/5)∠−53.1° = 0.2∠−53.1° S, which in rectangular form is the same 0.12 − j0.16 S. When the impedance is inductive (positive imaginary part), the imaginary part of the admittance (the susceptance) is negative.
choiceNotes: The sign of the imaginary part is reversed. For 1/(a + jb) you multiply by the complex conjugate, so the sign of the imaginary part flips.
This is 1/3 − j(1/4), taking the reciprocals of the real and imaginary parts separately, which is not how the reciprocal of a complex number is calculated.

question: In the parallel RLC circuit in the figure, the RMS currents in the resistor R, the coil L and the capacitor C are IR = 4 A, IL = 5 A and IC = 2 A. Which of the following is the RMS value of the current I drawn from the source?
explanation: Method 1 (complex numbers): taking the source voltage as the reference, IR is in phase, IL lags by 90° and IC leads by 90°, so I = 4 − j5 + j2 = 4 − j3 A. Its magnitude is √(4² + 3²) = 5 A. Method 2 (phasor diagram): IL and IC point in opposite directions, so only their difference of 3 A remains, and it combines at a right angle with the 4 A of IR to form a 3-4-5 right triangle. I lags the voltage by about 36.9°, and the circuit as a whole is inductive.
choiceNotes: Correct. |4 − j3| = 5 A.
4 + 5 − 2 = 7 A accounts for IL and IC cancelling, but adds the magnitudes while ignoring that IR is at a right angle to them.
This simply adds the magnitudes of the three currents. Currents with different phases must be added as phasors (vectors).

question: In the parallel RLC circuit in the figure, the source frequency is set to the resonant frequency f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)). Which of the following correctly describes the circuit?
choices: The impedance seen from the source is at its minimum, and the current drawn from the source is at its maximum
The current drawn from the source leads the source voltage by 90°
The currents in L and C cancel, so the current drawn from the source is only the current in R and is at its minimum
explanation: Method 1 (admittance): the admittance of the parallel circuit is Y = 1/R + j(ωC − 1/(ωL)); at f0 the imaginary part becomes 0 and |Y| takes its minimum value 1/R. The impedance takes its maximum value R, and the source current V/R is at its minimum and in phase with the voltage. Method 2 (phasor diagram): at f0, IL and IC are equal in size and opposite in direction, so they cancel and only IR remains in the source current. A large current circulates between L and C but is invisible to the source, which is why parallel resonant circuits are used as tank circuits that pick out a particular frequency.
choiceNotes: This describes series resonance. At parallel resonance the impedance is at its maximum and the source current at its minimum.
At resonance the currents in L and C cancel, so the source current is in phase with the voltage.
Correct. At parallel resonance the source current is only IR and is at its minimum.

question: As in figure (b), a balanced three-phase load is Δ-connected with an impedance of Z = 30 Ω per phase. If it is replaced by an equivalent Y connection as in figure (a) that draws the same line currents, which of the following is the impedance per phase?
explanation: Method 1 (Δ-Y conversion formula): if the sides of the Δ are Zab, Zbc and Zca, phase a of the Y is Za = Zab·Zca/(Zab + Zbc + Zca); for a balanced load this is 30 × 30/90 = 10 Ω, that is, Z/3. Method 2 (check with the line current): with a line voltage VL, the Δ connection has a phase current of VL/30 and a line current √3 times larger, √3 VL/30. In the Y connection the line current is the phase voltage VL/√3 divided by ZY, so (VL/√3)/ZY = √3 VL/30 gives ZY = 10 Ω.
choiceNotes: Correct. For a balanced load, ZY = ZΔ/3 = 10 Ω.
30/√3 ≈ 17 Ω wrongly applies the factor √3 between voltages or currents directly to the impedance. For impedance the factor √3 appears twice, giving one third.
Multiplying by 3 is the opposite conversion, used when turning a Y-connected Z into an equivalent Δ connection.

question: In the series RLC circuit in the figure, R = 10 Ω, ωL = 30 Ω, 1/(ωC) = 20 Ω and the source voltage is V = 100 V RMS. Which pair correctly gives the RMS value of the current I and its phase relative to the source voltage?
choices: About 1.7 A, in phase with the voltage
About 7.1 A, leads the voltage by 45°
About 7.1 A, lags the voltage by 45°
explanation: Method 1 (complex numbers): Z = R + j(ωL − 1/(ωC)) = 10 + j10 Ω, so I = 100/(10 + j10) = 5 − j5 A. Its magnitude is √(5² + 5²) ≈ 7.07 A and its angle is −45°, so the current lags the voltage by 45°. Method 2 (phasor diagram): taking the current as the reference, VR = 10I is in phase, VL = 30I leads by 90° and VC = 20I lags by 90°, so only the difference 10I remains as the reactive part. From |V| = √(10² + 10²) × I ≈ 14.1 × I = 100 V, I ≈ 7.1 A, and the voltage leads the current by 45°, that is, the current lags by 45°. Since ωL > 1/(ωC), the circuit is inductive.
choiceNotes: This is calculated with 10 + 30 + 20 = 60 Ω. Reactances are at right angles to resistance, and those of L and C are opposite, so their magnitudes cannot simply be added.
The magnitude is right, but the direction of the phase is reversed. In an inductive circuit with ωL > 1/(ωC), the current lags the voltage.
Correct. I = 5 − j5 A, that is, about 7.1 A lagging by 45°.

question: In the series RLC circuit in the figure, R = 10 Ω, L = 10 mH and C = 1 µF, and the frequency of a 1 V RMS sinusoidal voltage is set to the resonant frequency. Which of the following is the RMS voltage VC across the capacitor?
explanation: Method 1 (step-by-step from the resonance condition): the resonant angular frequency is ω0 = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(10×10⁻³ × 1×10⁻⁶) = 1×10⁴ rad/s (about 1.6 kHz). At resonance the reactances of L and C cancel, leaving only R, so I = 1 V/10 Ω = 0.1 A. The capacitor reactance is 1/(ω0C) = 100 Ω, so VC = 0.1 A × 100 Ω = 10 V. Method 2 (using the Q factor): a series resonant circuit has Q = (1/R)√(L/C) = (1/10) × √(10⁴) = 10, and at resonance the voltages across L and C are Q times the source voltage. VC = Q × 1 V = 10 V, which is larger than the source voltage, so the voltage ratings of the parts need attention.
choiceNotes: This is V/Q = 0.1 V, dividing where you should multiply by Q.
This is the voltage across R at resonance (equal to the 1 V source voltage). The voltages across L and C cancel each other, but neither one is 0.
Correct. VC = Q × V = 10 × 1 V = 10 V.

question: The voltage and current phasors (RMS) of a load are V = 100∠0° V and I = 5∠−30° A. Which of the following is the magnitude of the reactive power of this load?
explanation: Method 1 (from the power-factor angle): the current lags the voltage by 30°, so the active power is P = VI cos 30° ≈ 433 W and the reactive power is Q = VI sin 30° = 100 × 5 × 0.5 = 250 var. Method 2 (complex power): the complex power is S = V × (conjugate of I) = 100∠0° × 5∠30° = 500∠30° ≈ 433 + j250 VA; the real part is the active power and the imaginary part is the reactive power. The imaginary part is positive, so the load takes 250 var of lagging (inductive) reactive power. The apparent power is |S| = 500 VA.
choiceNotes: Correct. Q = VI sin 30° = 250 var.
VI cos 30° ≈ 433 is the active power [W], not the reactive power.
500 is the apparent power VI [VA], which ignores the phase difference.

question: A sinusoidal voltage of 100 V RMS is applied to a load consisting of a resistor R = 8 Ω in series with a coil of reactance X = 6 Ω. Which of the following is the active power of the load?
explanation: Method 1 (from the current): |Z| = √(8² + 6²) = 10 Ω, so I = 100/10 = 10 A, and the active power, consumed in the resistor, is P = I²R = 10² × 8 = 800 W. Method 2 (from the power factor): the power factor is cos φ = R/|Z| = 0.8, so P = VI cos φ = 100 × 10 × 0.8 = 800 W. Method 3 (complex power): S = V²/(conjugate of Z) = 10000/(8 − j6) = 800 + j600 VA, whose real part is 800 W. The coil's reactance consumes no power; 600 var of reactive power shuttles back and forth between it and the source.
choiceNotes: 600 is I²X, the reactive power [var].
Correct. P = I²R = 800 W.
1,000 is the apparent power VI [VA].

question: As in the figure, a capacitor C is connected in parallel with an inductive load of 8 kW active power and a power factor of 0.8 (lagging) so that the power factor seen from the source becomes 1. Which of the following is the reactive power the capacitor must supply?
explanation: Method 1 (power triangle): the apparent power is S = P/cos φ = 8/0.8 = 10 kVA, and the reactive power is Q = √(S² − P²) = √(10² − 8²) = 6 kvar. To raise the power factor to 1, the capacitor must supply 6.0 kvar of leading reactive power, cancelling all of this lagging reactive power. Method 2 (using tan φ): Q = P tan φ, and for cos φ = 0.8, tan φ = 0.6/0.8 = 0.75, so Q = 8 × 0.75 = 6 kvar. At 200 V and 50 Hz the required capacitance is C = Q/(ωV²) = 6000/(2π × 50 × 200²) ≈ 477 µF. The active power of the load is unchanged, and the source current falls from 10 kVA/200 V = 50 A to 8 kW/200 V = 40 A.
choiceNotes: Correct. It cancels Q = P tan φ = 6 kvar.
8.0 is the value of the active power [kW]; the capacitor does not cancel active power.
10 is the value of the apparent power [kVA].

question: As in the figure, a capacitor C is connected in parallel with an inductive load of 8 kW active power and a power factor of 0.8 (lagging) to improve the power factor seen from the source to 0.96 (lagging). Which of the following is closest to the reactive power the capacitor must supply?
explanation: Method 1 (difference of tan φ): the reactive power before correction is Q1 = P tan φ1 = 8 × 0.75 = 6 kvar. After correction, cos φ2 = 0.96 gives sin φ2 = 0.28 and tan φ2 = 0.28/0.96 ≈ 0.292, so Q2 = 8 × 0.292 ≈ 2.33 kvar. The capacitor's reactive power is Qc = Q1 − Q2 ≈ 6 − 2.33 ≈ 3.7 kvar. Method 2 (power triangle): the apparent power after correction is 8/0.96 ≈ 8.33 kVA, and Q2 = √(8.33² − 8²) ≈ 2.33 kvar, the same result. Raising the power factor all the way to 1 would need 6 kvar, but for 0.96 a capacitor of about 60% of that size is enough.
choiceNotes: About 2.3 kvar is the reactive power Q2 that remains after correction, not the amount the capacitor supplies.
Correct. Qc = 6 − 2.33 ≈ 3.7 kvar.
6.0 kvar is the value for raising the power factor to 1.

question: A Δ-connected load with a 20 Ω resistor in each phase, as in figure (b), is connected to a balanced three-phase source with a line voltage of 200 V RMS. Which of the following is closest to the RMS line current?
explanation: Method 1 (Δ relations): in a Δ connection the line voltage appears directly across each phase resistor, so the phase current is 200/20 = 10 A. A line current is the phasor difference of two phase currents, and its magnitude is √3 times the phase current: 10√3 ≈ 17.3 A. Method 2 (convert to Y): the equivalent Y has 20/3 Ω per phase, and dividing the phase voltage 200/√3 ≈ 115.5 V by 6.67 Ω gives a line current of about 17.3 A. Method 3 (check with power): the total power of the load is 3 × 10² × 20 = 6 kW, and P = √3 VL IL gives IL = 6000/(√3 × 200) ≈ 17.3 A.
choiceNotes: 10/√3 ≈ 5.8 A divides by √3 where you should multiply. In a Δ connection the line current is larger than the phase current.
10 A is the phase current (the current in each phase resistor).
Correct. The line current is √3 times the phase current, about 17 A.

question: A Y-connected load with an impedance of Z = 8 + j6 Ω per phase, as in figure (a), is connected to a balanced three-phase source with a line voltage of 200 V RMS. Which of the following is closest to the total three-phase active power?
explanation: Method 1 (one phase times 3): the phase voltage of the Y is 200/√3 ≈ 115.5 V and |Z| = √(8² + 6²) = 10 Ω, so the phase current (= line current) is about 11.55 A. The active power of one phase is I²R = 11.55² × 8 ≈ 1067 W, and for three phases 3 × 1067 ≈ 3200 W = 3.2 kW. Method 2 (three-phase power formula): the power factor is cos φ = 8/10 = 0.8, so P = √3 × VL × IL × cos φ = √3 × 200 × 11.55 × 0.8 ≈ 3.2 kW. Method 3 (simplify the formula): P = 3 × (VL/√3)² × R/|Z|² = VL² × R/|Z|² = 200² × 8/100 = 3200 W, which can be calculated without √3 at all.
choiceNotes: About 1.1 kW is the power of one phase. The total for three phases is three times that.
Correct. P = √3 VL IL cos φ ≈ 3.2 kW.
9.6 kW is calculated by applying the 200 V line voltage directly to each phase, which corresponds to the power of the same load connected in Δ.

question: As in the figure, a load impedance ZL is connected to terminals a-b of an AC circuit whose Thevenin equivalent voltage is Vth = 10 V RMS and internal impedance Zth = 3 + j4 Ω. If both the resistance and the reactance of ZL can be chosen freely, which of the following is closest to the maximum power consumed by the load?
explanation: Method 1 (conjugate matching): choosing ZL as the complex conjugate of Zth, 3 − j4 Ω, cancels the reactances, so the circuit impedance is just a 6 Ω resistance. The current is 10/6 ≈ 1.67 A and the load power is (10/6)² × 3 ≈ 8.3 W. In general, Pmax = Vth²/(4Rth) = 100/12 ≈ 8.3 W. Method 2 (maximize the formula): with ZL = RL + jXL, P = Vth² RL/((3 + RL)² + (4 + XL)²); first set XL = −4 Ω to remove the reactive part of the denominator, then choose RL = 3 Ω, which maximizes RL/(3 + RL)², giving the same result.
choiceNotes: This is the case ZL = Zth = 3 + j4 Ω. The reactances do not cancel, the current stays at 1 A, and the power is 3 W.
This is the value for a resistive load equal to |Zth| = 5 Ω. It is the maximum when the reactance cannot be chosen, but when it can, conjugate matching gives more.
Correct. Conjugate matching gives Pmax = Vth²/(4Rth) ≈ 8.3 W.

question: A sine wave of angular frequency ω = 1/(RC) is applied to the RC high-pass filter in figure (b). Which of the following correctly describes the amplitude and phase of the output relative to the input?
choices: The amplitude is about 0.71 times, and the output lags the input by 45°
The amplitude is about 0.71 times, and the output leads the input by 45°
The amplitude is 0.5 times, and the output is in phase with the input
explanation: Method 1 (complex numbers): the transfer function is H(jω) = jωRC/(1 + jωRC), and for ωRC = 1, H = j/(1 + j) = (1 + j)/2. Its magnitude is 1/√2 ≈ 0.71 (−3 dB) and its angle is +45°, so the output leads the input by 45°. Method 2 (phasor diagram): the current in the series RC circuit leads the input voltage because the circuit is capacitive, and at ω = 1/(RC), R and 1/(ωC) are equal, so the lead is exactly 45°. The output is the voltage across R, which is in phase with the current, so the output also leads the input by 45°. At the same frequency, the output of the low-pass filter in figure (a) lags by 45°.

question: In the parallel RLC circuit in the figure, R = 20 kΩ, L = 1 mH and C = 10 nF. Near the resonant frequency, which of the following is closest to the difference between the two frequencies at which the magnitude of the circuit impedance falls to 1/√2 of its value at resonance (the bandwidth)?
explanation: Method 1 (from the Q factor): the resonant frequency is f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)) ≈ 50.3 kHz. The Q of a parallel resonant circuit is Q = R√(C/L) = 20×10³ × √(10×10⁻⁹/1×10⁻³) ≈ 63.2, so the bandwidth is BW = f0/Q ≈ 50.3 kHz/63.2 ≈ 796 Hz. Method 2 (directly from the admittance): the two angular frequencies at which the magnitude of the imaginary part of Y = 1/R + j(ωC − 1/(ωL)) equals the real part 1/R differ by 1/(RC), so BW = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 20×10³ × 10×10⁻⁹) ≈ 796 Hz. In parallel resonance, the larger R is, the higher the Q and the narrower the bandwidth.
choiceNotes: Correct. BW = 1/(2πRC) ≈ 796 Hz.
About 50 kHz is the resonant frequency f0 itself.
About 3.2 MHz applies the series-resonance formula BW = R/(2πL). In parallel resonance the role of R is reversed, and Q = R√(C/L).

question: In the circuit in the figure, E = 12 V, R1 = 4 Ω, R2 = 12 Ω and the current source is J = 2 A (flowing into node A). Which of the following is the voltage VA of node A with respect to ground?
explanation: Applying Kirchhoff's current law at node A and setting the currents flowing out through R1 and R2 equal to the incoming current J gives (VA − 12)/4 + VA/12 = 2. Multiplying both sides by 12 gives 3VA − 36 + VA = 24, so VA = 60/4 = 15 V. Checking with the superposition theorem, E alone contributes 12 × 12/(4 + 12) = 9 V and J alone contributes 2 A × 3 Ω (R1 and R2 in parallel) = 6 V, for a total of 15 V. The node voltage is higher than the source voltage E because the current pushed in by J flows through R1 toward E.
choiceNotes: This is the contribution of the current source J alone (with E shorted); the contribution of E is missing.
This is the voltage-divider result for the voltage source E alone (with J open); the contribution of J is missing.
Correct. The node equation gives VA = 15 V.

question: The circuit in the figure contains a current-controlled voltage source that produces a voltage r·i (r = 3 Ω) proportional to the current i in R1. With E = 10 V and R1 = 2 Ω, which of the following is the Thevenin equivalent resistance Rth seen from terminals a-b?
explanation: The voltage at terminal a is E minus the voltages across R1 and the dependent source: Va = 10 − 2i − 3i = 10 − 5i. With the terminals open, i = 0, so the open-circuit voltage is 10 V; with them shorted, 10 − 5i = 0 gives a current of 2 A, so Rth = 10/2 = 5 Ω. Setting E to 0 and applying a voltage V to the terminals gives V = −5i, so V/(−i) = 5 Ω as well. A dependent source takes its value from a current in the circuit, so it must not be set to 0 the way an independent source is.
choiceNotes: This is 2 − 3 = −1 Ω, taking the dependent source in the opposite direction (aiding E). In the figure, i enters the + side, so the source acts as a voltage drop.
This sets the dependent source to 0 (shorted) like an independent source and sees only R1.
Correct. Voc/Isc = 10 V/2 A = 5 Ω.

question: In a linear circuit with two sources, which of the following cannot be found with the superposition theorem by applying the sources one at a time and adding the results?
choices: The power consumed in a resistor
explanation: The superposition theorem holds because voltages and currents are proportional to the sources (the circuit is linear). Power is proportional to the square of the current, so adding the powers due to each source is wrong. For example, if one source drives 1 A and the other 2 A in the same direction through a 1 Ω resistor, the correct power is (1 + 2)² × 1 = 9 W, but adding the separate powers gives 1 + 4 = 5 W. To find a power, first find the current by superposition and then square it.
choiceNotes: Correct. Power is proportional to the square of the current and is not linear.
Current is proportional to the sources, so it can be found by superposition.
Node voltages are also proportional to the sources, so they can be found by superposition.

question: In a linear resistive circuit whose only sources are two DC voltage sources E1 and E2, the voltage Vo across a resistor is measured. With E1 = 1 V and E2 = 0 V, Vo = 2 V; with E1 = 0 V and E2 = 1 V, Vo = −1 V. Which of the following is Vo when E1 = 3 V and E2 = 2 V?
explanation: In a linear circuit the output can be written as a sum of terms proportional to each source, Vo = aE1 + bE2 (the superposition theorem and proportionality). The measurements give a = 2 and b = −1, so Vo = 2 × 3 + (−1) × 2 = 4 V. The answer follows from linearity alone, without knowing what is inside the circuit.
choiceNotes: 2 + (−1) = 1 V just adds the two measured values without scaling each in proportion to the source size (3 times and 2 times).
Correct. Vo = 2E1 − E2 = 4 V.
This takes the term due to E2 as positive, giving 6 + 2 = 8 V.

question: Treating the T network in the figure as a two-port with R1 = 2 Ω, R2 = 3 Ω and R3 = 6 Ω, which of the following is the correct set of Z parameters (V1 = z11 I1 + z12 I2, V2 = z21 I1 + z22 I2)?
explanation: z11 is the impedance V1/I1 seen from the input with the output open (I2 = 0): R1 and R3 in series, 2 + 6 = 8 Ω. z12 is V1/I2 with the input open (I1 = 0); I2 flows through R2 and R3, and the voltage across R3 appears directly as V1, so z12 = R3 = 6 Ω. Likewise z22 = R2 + R3 = 9 Ω and z21 = z12 = 6 Ω; in a circuit made only of passive elements, z12 = z21 (reciprocity) holds.
choiceNotes: This leaves out R3, which is common to z11 and z22. Even with the other port open, there is a current path through R3.
This adds all three resistances. No current flows in the resistor on the open side (R2 for z11).
Correct. z11 = 8 Ω, z12 = 6 Ω and z22 = 9 Ω.

question: In the RC circuit in the figure, a DC voltage E is applied to an uncharged capacitor by closing the switch at t = 0. With the time constant τ = RC, which of the following is closest to the capacitor voltage vC at t = 5τ, as a percentage of the final value E?
explanation: Method 1 (substitute into the formula): the capacitor voltage is vC(t) = E(1 − e^(−t/τ)), so at t = 5τ it is 1 − e^(−5) ≈ 1 − 0.0067 = 0.993, about 99.3%. In theory it never reaches 100%, so in practice the transient response is considered finished after about 5τ.
choiceNotes: About 95% is the value at t = 3τ.

question: In the RC circuit in the figure, E = 10 V, R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 µF, and the capacitor is initially uncharged. Which of the following is closest to the capacitor voltage vC 2 seconds after the switch is closed at t = 0?
explanation: Method 1 (differential equation): the circuit equation is RC dvC/dt + vC = E, and its solution with vC(0) = 0 is vC(t) = E(1 − e^(−t/RC)). Since τ = RC = 10×10³ × 100×10⁻⁶ = 1 s, vC(2) = 10(1 − e^(−2)) ≈ 10 × 0.865 ≈ 8.6 V. Method 2 (Laplace transform): in the s-domain, VC(s) = (E/s) × (1/(sC))/(R + 1/(sC)) = E/(s(1 + sRC)), which splits into partial fractions as E(1/s − 1/(s + 1/RC)) and transforms back to the same formula. Method 3 (time-constant rule of thumb): 63% at 1τ, and at 2τ a further 63% of the remaining 37% is added, reaching about 86%, so about 8.6 V can be estimated.
choiceNotes: About 6.3 V is the value at t = τ = 1 s.
About 9.5 V is the value at t = 3τ = 3 s.

question: In the RC circuit in the figure, E = 10 V, R = 2 kΩ and C = 1 µF, and the capacitor is initially charged to 4 V with its + side in the figure at the higher potential. Which of the following is closest to the current i one time constant τ after the switch is closed at t = 0?
explanation: Method 1 (initial and final values): the capacitor voltage cannot change suddenly, so at t = 0+ it is still vC = 4 V and i(0+) = (10 − 4)/2 kΩ = 3 mA. After a long time i = 0, and in between the current changes exponentially with the time constant τ = RC = 2 ms, so i(t) = 3e^(−t/τ) mA and i(τ) = 3 × e^(−1) ≈ 1.1 mA. Method 2 (Laplace transform): representing the capacitor as 1/(sC) in series with a voltage source V0/s gives I(s) = ((E − V0)/s)/(R + 1/(sC)) = ((E − V0)/R)/(s + 1/(RC)), whose inverse transform is the same i(t). Method 3 (differential equation): solving RC dvC/dt + vC = E with vC(0) = 4 V gives vC = 10 − 6e^(−t/τ), and i = C dvC/dt gives the same formula.
choiceNotes: Correct. i(τ) = 3 mA × e^(−1) ≈ 1.1 mA.
About 1.8 mA ignores the initial voltage: (10 V/2 kΩ) × e^(−1).
3.0 mA is the current just after the switch closes, at t = 0+.

All of the source current flows into the capacitor, so i(0+) = E/R1 = 12/2 = 6 A. After a long time the capacitor acts like an open circuit and the coil like a short, so i = 12/(2 + 4) = 2 A and vC is the voltage across R2, 2 × 4 = 8 V. Method 2 (Laplace transform with the initial- and final-value theorems): with the impedance seen from the source Z(s) = R1 + (sL + R2 in parallel with 1/(sC)), I(s) = E/(s Z(s)). As s → ∞, Z → R1, so i(0+) = E/R1; as s → 0, Z → R1 + R2, so i(∞) = E/(R1 + R2), the same results.
choiceNotes: 12 V assumes the coil still blocks current after a long time, so the full source voltage appears across the capacitor. Just after switching, the capacitor voltage is 0, so the capacitor acts like a short and current flows.
2 A is the current after a long time, not just after switching.

question: In the series RLC circuit in the figure, L = 1 mH and C = 0.1 µF. Which of the following is the resistance R that gives critical damping, in which the step response approaches the final value fastest without oscillating?
explanation: Method 1 (characteristic equation): from the circuit equation L di/dt + Ri + (1/C)∫i dt = E, the characteristic equation is Ls² + Rs + 1/C = 0. The condition for a double root (zero discriminant) is R² = 4L/C, so R = 2√(L/C) = 2 × √(1×10⁻³/0.1×10⁻⁶) = 2 × 100 = 200 Ω. Method 2 (damping ratio): comparing with the standard form s² + 2ζωn s + ωn² gives ζ = (R/2)√(C/L), and critical damping ζ = 1 gives the same R = 2√(L/C) = 200 Ω. A smaller R gives a damped oscillation, and a larger R gives overdamping.
choiceNotes: √(L/C) = 100 Ω forgets the factor of 2. This value gives a damped oscillation with ζ = 0.5.
Correct. R = 2√(L/C) = 200 Ω.

question: In the series RLC circuit in the figure, L = 1 mH, C = 0.1 µF and R = 50 Ω. Which pair correctly gives the damping ratio ζ and the type of step response?
explanation: Method 1 (compare with the standard form): the characteristic equation is s² + (R/L)s + 1/(LC) = 0, and comparing it with the standard form s² + 2ζωn s + ωn² gives ωn = 1/√(LC) = 1×10⁵ rad/s and 2ζωn = R/L. From these, ζ = (R/2)√(C/L) = 25 × √(0.1×10⁻⁶/1×10⁻³) = 25 × 0.01 = 0.25. Method 2 (ratio to the critical resistance): the resistance for critical damping is 2√(L/C) = 200 Ω, so ζ = R/(2√(L/C)) = 50/200 = 0.25 as well. Since ζ < 1, the step response overshoots the final value and settles while oscillating: a damped oscillation.

question: In the series RLC circuit in the figure, L = 1 mH, C = 0.1 µF and R = 50 Ω. Which of the following is closest to the frequency of the damped oscillation that appears in the step response?
explanation: Method 1 (roots of the characteristic equation): the roots of Ls² + Rs + 1/C = 0 are s = −α ± jωd, with α = R/(2L) = 50/(2 × 10⁻³) = 2.5×10⁴ s⁻¹ and ωn = 1/√(LC) = 1×10⁵ rad/s. ωd = √(ωn² − α²) = √(10¹⁰ − 6.25×10⁸) ≈ 9.68×10⁴ rad/s, so fd = ωd/(2π) ≈ 15.4 kHz. Method 2 (from the damping ratio): ζ = α/ωn = 0.25, so ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²) = 10⁵ × √0.9375 ≈ 9.68×10⁴ rad/s, the same result. The response oscillates at this frequency while decaying inside the envelope e^(−αt).
choiceNotes: Correct. fd = ωn√(1 − ζ²)/(2π) ≈ 15.4 kHz.
About 15.9 kHz is the natural frequency fn = ωn/(2π); it ignores the drop in frequency due to damping.
100 kHz mistakes ωn = 1×10⁵ rad/s for a value in Hz.

question: In the series RLC circuit in the figure, R = 5 Ω, L = 1 H and C = 0.25 F. Which pair correctly gives the roots of the characteristic equation and the type of step response?
explanation: Method 1 (characteristic equation): substituting the values into Ls² + Rs + 1/C = 0 gives s² + 5s + 4 = 0, and (s + 1)(s + 4) = 0 gives two distinct negative real roots, s = −1 and −4. Method 2 (damping ratio): ωn = 1/√(LC) = 2 rad/s and ζ = (R/2)√(C/L) = 2.5 × 0.5 = 1.25; since ζ > 1, the response is overdamped. The discriminant R² − 4L/C = 25 − 16 = 9 > 0 confirms this.

This attaches ωn = 2 directly as the imaginary part to the real part −R/(2L) = −2.5. The imaginary part is √(ωn² − α²), and here ωn < α, so there is no imaginary part.
Correct. s = −1 and −4, overdamped.

question: In the series RLC circuit in the figure, E = 6 V, R = 4 Ω, L = 1 H and C = 1/3 F, and all initial values are 0. Which of the following is the current i(t) [A] after the switch is closed at t = 0?
explanation: Method 1 (Laplace transform and partial fractions): in the s-domain, I(s) = (E/s)/(R + sL + 1/(sC)) = 6/(s² + 4s + 3) = 6/((s + 1)(s + 3)). Splitting into partial fractions as I(s) = A/(s + 1) + B/(s + 3) gives A = 6/(−1 + 3) = 3 and B = 6/(−3 + 1) = −3, so i(t) = 3e^(−t) − 3e^(−3t) A. Method 2 (differential equation): the roots −1 and −3 of the characteristic equation s² + 4s + 3 = 0 give i = Ae^(−t) + Be^(−3t); i(0+) = 0 (continuity of the coil current) and di/dt(0+) = E/L = 6 A/s give A + B = 0 and −A − 3B = 6, so A = 3 and B = −3. The current peaks at about 1.15 A at t = (ln 3)/2 ≈ 0.55 s and returns to 0 as the capacitor charges.
choiceNotes: At t = 0 this gives i = 6 A, which contradicts the coil current starting from 0.
Correct. i(t) = 3e^(−t) − 3e^(−3t), with i(0) = 0.
This forgets to divide by (s + 3) − (s + 1) = 2 when finding the partial-fraction coefficients.

question: Which of the following is the s-domain impedance Z(s) of a resistor R and a capacitor C connected in parallel?
explanation: Method 1 (sum of admittances): in the s-domain, the impedance of a capacitor is 1/(sC) and its admittance is sC. In parallel the admittances add, so Y(s) = 1/R + sC = (1 + sRC)/R and Z(s) = R/(1 + sRC). Method 2 (product over sum): multiplying the numerator and denominator of Z = R × (1/(sC))/(R + 1/(sC)) by sC also gives R/(1 + sRC). Setting s = jω gives the AC impedance R/(1 + jωRC); it approaches R as s → 0 (DC) and 0 as s → ∞.
choiceNotes: This is the impedance of R and C connected in series.
This dimensionless quantity has the form of the transfer function of an RC high-pass filter; it is not an impedance.
Correct. Z(s) = R/(1 + sRC).

Since RC = 1×10³ × 1×10⁻⁶ = 1×10⁻³ s, the pole is at s = −1,000 s⁻¹. Method 2 (link to the time response): a pole at s = −a corresponds to a term e^(−at) in the step response and other responses, so from the RC circuit response e^(−t/RC) the pole reads −1/τ = −1/(1 ms). The magnitude of the pole, 1,000 rad/s, is the cutoff angular frequency, about 159 Hz as a frequency.

159 is the number for the cutoff frequency 1000/(2π) ≈ 159 Hz. Poles in the s-plane are expressed in units of angular frequency (s⁻¹ = rad/s).

question: Which of the following correctly represents, in an s-domain circuit including its initial condition, a capacitor C charged to a voltage V0 at time t = 0?
choices: An impedance 1/(sC) with a voltage source V0 in series
An impedance 1/(sC) with a current source V0/s in parallel
An impedance 1/(sC) with a voltage source V0/s in series
explanation: Method 1 (from the transform of a derivative): taking the Laplace transform of i = C dv/dt with the derivative rule L[dv/dt] = sV(s) − v(0) gives I(s) = sCV(s) − CV0. Solving for V(s) gives V(s) = I(s)/(sC) + V0/s: 1/(sC) in series with a voltage source V0/s (the transform of the constant voltage V0). Method 2 (equivalent parallel form): the same equation read as I(s) = sCV(s) − CV0 can also be represented as 1/(sC) in parallel with a current source CV0 (the transform of an impulse current CV0δ(t)). The initial current I0 of a coil is likewise represented by sL in series with a voltage source LI0.
choiceNotes: The value of the voltage source must also be transformed to the s-domain. A constant V0 in the time domain becomes V0/s in the s-domain.
In the parallel form, the value of the current source is CV0. With V0/s even the units do not match.
Correct. 1/(sC) in series with a voltage source V0/s.

question: The Laplace transform of a voltage in a circuit is V(s) = 10(s + 3)/(s(s + 2)(s + 5)). Which of the following is the voltage v(∞) after a long time?
explanation: Method 1 (final-value theorem): v(∞) = lim(s→0) sV(s) = 10 × 3/(2 × 5) = 3 V. The theorem can be used when all the poles of sV(s) are in the left half-plane (the response converges). Method 2 (check with partial fractions): writing V(s) = A/s + B/(s + 2) + C/(s + 5) gives A = 3, B = −5/3 and C = −4/3, so v(t) = 3 − (5/3)e^(−2t) − (4/3)e^(−5t). As t → ∞ the exponential terms vanish, leaving 3 V, and at t = 0 the value is 3 − 5/3 − 4/3 = 0, which agrees with the initial-value theorem lim(s→∞) sV(s) = 0.
choiceNotes: 0 V is the initial value v(0+) = lim(s→∞) sV(s).
Correct. lim(s→0) sV(s) = 3 V.
